newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern, Conrail, CSX to meet Friday.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern, Conrail, CSX to meet Friday.

text.p: The top executives of Conrail Inc., CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. will meet Friday in a major step aimed a resolving a stalemate in the three-month takeover battle for Philadelphia-based Conrail.

Norfolk Southern Chief Executive Officer David Goode announced the meeting Wednesday as he gathered with Wall Street analysts to discuss the railroad's fourth-quarter earnings. The railroad reported a 13 percent rise in profit for the quarter.

Goode declined to disclose any details about the meeting with Conrail Chief Executive David LeVan and CSX Chief Executive John Snow. Sources close to the companies earlier this week said only Goode, LeVan and Snow were expected to attend.
"We have set a meeting Friday, and I plan to be there, ready to work hard for a solution," Goode said.
Conrail and Richmond, Va.-based CSX could not be reached for comment on the meeting.

Conrail has repeatedly said it is committed to its proposed $9.5 billion merger with CSX despite a rival $10.3 billion bid from Norfolk Southern. Conrail shareholders earlier this month defeated a key provision that would have permitted the planned merger to move forward.
Meanwhile, Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern is in the process of buying 9.9 percent of Conrail's stock.

Goode also reiterated that he would not accept any type of resolution to the stalemate unless it valued Conrail at Norfolk Southern's bid of $115 per share, but added, "I'm going in with a completely open mind."
He admitted that the talks would be difficult, but said he remained optimistic about the outcome.

"I go prepared, on my own part, to negotiate hard, to negotiate fairly and to negotiate to reach a reasonable solution. I am confident others will do the same," he said at a news conference after the meeting with analysts.

Last week, executives of the three railroads agreed to hold discussions about the planned Conrail-CSX deal. Sources close to the companies said attorneys hammered out confidentiality agreements for the executives over the weekend.
Although he initially spoke only with CSX's Snow by telephone, Goode said at the news conference that he has since spoken with LeVan of Conrail. He did not discuss the nature of the conversation.
Some Wall Street experts have speculated that the ultimate conclusion will call for a splitting up of Conrail's assets.
But sources close to Conrail have said its executives would oppose plans to split up the railroad and distribute its pieces to CSX and Norfolk Southern.
In its earnings report, Norfolk Southern said strong rail traffic and tight expense controls offset higher fuel costs.
It said net income rose to $200.5 million, or $1.60 a share, from $176.9 million, or $1.37 a share, in the 1995 quarter. Sales rose 2 percent to $1.18 billion from $1.16 billion.
"Despite an extraordinary rise in fuel prices, we ended 1996 on a high note, setting records across the board," Goode said in a statement.
He cited strength in shipments of cars, coal and chemicals and noted the company's North American Van Lines trucking unit had its best operating earnings in nine years.
Transportation expenses actually fell 3 percent in the quarter despite higher fuel costs, Norfolk Southern said.

Norfolk Southern stock rose $2.125 to $88.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock of Conrail rose 87.5 cents to $106.75 and CSX shares gained 37.5 cents to $46.75, also on NYSE.
